s: Part one.
Designing tool interfaces.
By the end of this part, you'll know how to write a tool description the model can actually use.
When to rename, when to split, and when to merge tools.
And why the strongest guarantee is a tool the agent simply doesn't have.
Let's start with a picture.
You're going somewhere with no phone signal.
You leave a note for the person looking after your house.
"Feed the cat."
That's accurate.
And it will still go wrong.
Now try this version.
"Half a cup of the dry food in the pantry, twice a day.
She will act starving regardless.
The tins in the fridge belong to the neighbour's cat."
That version survives your absence.
The difference isn't effort, or politeness.
The note has to answer the questions the sitter would otherwise ask you.
Because asking is not on offer.
A tool description is that note.
The technical name for what the model sees is the tool definition.
It has a name, a description, and an input schema.
And each parameter carries its own description.
Anthropic's own documentation is blunt about this.
Detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance.
The documented floor is at least three to four sentences per tool.
More if the tool is complex.
So what does a good description cover?
Seven things.
One.
What the tool does.
Two.
When to reach for it.
Three.
When not to.
Four.
What each parameter means, in terms someone can act on.
Five.
What shape the result comes back in.
Six.
How recent, and how complete, the data is.
Seven.
What the tool does not return.
In exam terms, here's the trap.
Thinking that description length is verbosity.
It isn't.
Once the description is the only thing available at the moment of choosing, length is coverage.
Anything you leave out becomes a guess.
And the guess happens quickly, repeatedly, and with nobody watching.
Hold on to this line.
The description is the interface, and the model knows only what you wrote.
Now the single most tested sentence in a description.
It's also the one architects skip most often.
Picture a shop sign that just says "Groceries."
You wander the aisles looking for stamps.
Now picture a sign that says "Groceries.
No post office counter, that is next door."
That one sends you to the right place first time.
Telling people what you don't do is as useful as telling them what you do.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A support agent has a tool called order_status_get.
Its description says only "Returns order status."
When customers ask where their parcel is, the agent calls order_status_get two or three times, with rephrased arguments, before giving up.
Yet carrier tracking lives in a separate tool, called shipment_tracking_get.
Tracking is needed in about one conversation in ten.
And the carrier's service is slow, and billed per call.
What best reduces the redundant calls?
Take a second.
The answer.
Rewrite the description.
It lists the fields the tool returns.
That's status, placed date, and line items, for one order.
It says plainly that it does not return carrier tracking or a delivery estimate.
And it points to shipment_tracking_get for those.
The technical name is a negative boundary, plus a named next hop.
Why were there repeated calls at all?
Because the agent keeps hoping the missing data will appear.
The boundary sentence ends that hope.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: merge the two tools into a single order_status_get that always calls the carrier and returns everything.
Why?
Consolidation is a real pattern.
But it suits tools that are always called together.
Here, tracking is needed one time in ten.
So the other nine conversations would pay for a slow, billed call they never needed.
The constraint words that decide it are "about one conversation in ten" and "slow and billed per call."
When you hear "rarely needed" or "expensive upstream," don't merge.
Wrong: add a rule to the system prompt saying tracking questions must use shipment_tracking_get.
Why?
That patches a description defect with prompt text.
And prompt text competes with everything else in the model's context.
The description is what the model reads at the moment it chooses a tool.
So fix the defect where selection actually happens.
Wrong: force shipment_tracking_get with the tool_choice setting, whenever the customer mentions parcel, tracking or delivery.
Why? tool_choice is a per-request lever, not a keyword router.
Wrapping keyword logic around it papers over the description problem.
And it misfires on messages that mention delivery for other reasons.
Hold on to this line.
Say what the tool does not return, and name the tool that does.
Next, two tools that sound alike.
Picture two kitchen drawers, both labelled "Utensils."
You open whichever is nearer, and hope.
Now relabel them.
"Cooking spoons and spatulas."
And "Table cutlery, spatulas are in the other drawer."
Nobody opens the wrong one again.
You could also hire someone to stand by the drawers and direct traffic.
It would work.
And it's an expensive answer to a labelling problem.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A research agent has two tools. search_web, described as "Searches for information."
And search_documents, described as "Searches documents for information."
For questions about the company's internal policies, the agent alternates between them almost at random.
And web results sometimes contradict internal policy.
The team has one week.
It wants the lowest-complexity fix that addresses the cause.
Take a second.
The answer.
Rename them to search_public_web and search_internal_policies.
And give each description its corpus, and a pointer to the other.
The technical terms here are namespacing, and mutually exclusive boundaries.
Why does renaming work?
A name with real meaning narrows selection before the description is even read.
Good practice is to namespace by service, then by resource.
So jira_issues_search sits beside jira_users_search and github_pulls_search.
And the model narrows by prefix.
A note on naming rules.
The Claude Developer Platform requires tool names made of letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, up to sixty-four characters.
M C P itself allows up to one hundred and twenty-eight, and also permits a dot.
So design to the narrower rule.
That keeps your tools portable.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: move each search tool into its own subagent, under a coordinator.
Why?
That adds a coordination layer and a handoff, to fix overlapping wording.
Wrong: add a routing classifier in front of the agent.
Why?
That's the high-complexity last resort.
And the one-week, lowest-complexity constraint rules it out.
Wrong: set tool_choice to any on research turns.
Why?
It forces the agent to call a search tool.
But it still has to choose between two indistinguishable ones.
Hold on to this line.
Forcing a call never makes the right call.
There's a close cousin of this question in the study notes.
A support server has lookup, described as "Look up a customer."
And lookup_v2, described as "Look up a customer with the new schema."
The agent picks the legacy one about half the time, and gets stale data.
A developer proposes a system prompt paragraph saying lookup_v2 is always correct.
That's the weaker fix.
Why?
Because the ambiguity lives in the tool catalog.
And the model consults the catalog at selection time.
The strong fix has two moves.
Retire lookup entirely, removing the candidate.
And rename lookup_v2 to a descriptive, namespaced name, with a full description.
Hold on to this line.
When two tools sound alike, fix the names and boundaries before you touch the architecture.
A third flavour.
A custom tool losing to a built-in one.
Picture a new restaurant opening next to a famous one.
Its sign reads only "Food."
Everybody keeps going to the place they already know.
Then the sign changes.
It now reads "slow-cooked stews, better than next door when you want something hearty."
And the right diners start walking in.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A team built a custom M C P tool called code_semantic_search.
It's described as "Tool to search through the codebase."
For intent questions, such as "where do we retry failed payments," the agent almost always uses the built-in Grep instead.
And it misses logic that never uses the word retry.
The team wants the agent to keep using Grep for exact-string lookups.
What should they do first?
Take a second.
The answer.
Rewrite the description.
Four things go in.
It finds code by what it does, not by exact words.
It returns file paths, line numbers and snippets, ranked by relevance.
Use it instead of Grep when the question describes behaviour or intent.
And don't use it for exact strings or symbol names, because Grep is faster there.
Why does this matter?
Custom tools compete with built-in tools for selection.
And a one-line description loses that competition.
Now the wrong turns.
These teach you a ranking the exam calls on again and again.
Wrong: remove Grep, so the custom tool is the only option.
Why?
It violates the stated constraint that Grep must stay for exact lookups.
Wrong: add few-shot examples to the system prompt.
That means worked examples of which question goes to which tool.
Why is it wrong here?
It's a legitimate move.
But it's the second move.
It comes after the description says when to prefer the tool.
Wrong: add a routing subagent that classifies each question.
Why?
That's architecture to fix a language problem.
And it comes last.
So here's the order to remember for misrouting.
Four steps.
First.
Rename and split.
Second.
Expand the descriptions.
Third.
Add examples.
And only then, fourth.
Consider classifiers, or new architecture.
The word "first" in a stem is your cue to reach for the top of that ladder.
Hold on to this line.
A custom tool that loses to a built-in needs a better sign before it needs a bouncer.
Now the judgment the exam likes most.
When to split a tool, and when to merge tools.
It's a favourite because both directions fail.
Too many narrow tools make selection ambiguous.
And they force the agent to chain calls.
One broad tool becomes what the notes call a god-tool.
Its description cannot honestly explain everything it does.
So what's the underlying rule?
Shape tools around the decisions an agent makes.
Not around the endpoints your platform happens to expose.
Anthropic's own example: build one schedule_event tool.
Rather than shipping list_users, list_events and create_event, and hoping the agent assembles them.
When do you merge?
Three situations.
First.
When several tools are always called in sequence to answer one question.
One tool that runs the sequence removes the chaining turns, and the chance of stopping halfway.
Second.
When operations share one resource and differ only in the verb.
Like creating, reviewing and merging a pull request.
Those can sit behind a single tool, with an action parameter.
Third.
When a tool exists only because an interface happens to have that endpoint.
The study notes give a vivid example of that third one.
A logistics server registers thirty-eight tools, one per endpoint.
Creating a shipment takes over five model turns on average.
And in fourteen percent of sessions, the agent stops after fetching rates, and never creates the shipment.
The fix?
One create_shipment tool.
It works out carrier, service level, rate and address validation internally.
And you retire the intermediate tools.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: defer the thirty-eight definitions.
Why?
That would save context, but leave the five-hop workflow untouched.
Wrong: force tool calls.
Why?
That would keep the agent busy without ever reaching creation.
The technical name for the defect is an endpoint-mirroring catalog.
And when do you split?
Also three situations.
First.
When risk differs, like reading versus deleting.
Second.
When return shapes are incompatible, and the caller must branch on the result.
Third.
When a parameter is required only if another parameter takes a certain value.
That last one is a favourite.
Picture one paper form for both passport renewals and driving licences.
It carries a note: "fill in box seven only if you ticked driving licence."
People skip box seven constantly.
Now picture two separate forms, each demanding exactly its own boxes.
That stops the mistake before the form is handed in.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
An extraction pipeline has one tool, submit_document_fields.
It has a doc_type field that can be invoice or contract.
Line items are required only for invoices.
Governing law is required only for contracts.
So neither can be listed as required in the schema.
About twelve percent of calls omit the field their type needs, and fail downstream validation.
What's the best redesign?
Take a second.
The answer.
Split it into record_invoice_fields and record_contract_fields.
Each one marks its own type-specific fields as required.
Now, in the input schema, the required list can express each job honestly.
So an omission fails at validation, instead of downstream.
The notes also mention an action discriminator as an alternative pattern.
But in this item, the split is the answer.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a system prompt paragraph listing which fields each type needs.
Why?
It restates the rule without enforcing it.
Wrong: mark both fields required on every call.
Why?
It forces a value where none applies.
That pushes the model to invent a governing law for every invoice.
Wrong: a downstream validator that re-queues failures.
Why?
It catches the problem later, and more expensively.
And it leaves a schema that still cannot express the requirement.
Hold on to this line.
A conditionally required parameter means one tool is doing two jobs.
The other split trigger, risk, gets its own item.
And it connects to a principle that runs through the whole exam.
Picture a garage.
It gives its trainee one key that opens both the parts cupboard and the car lifts.
Then it pins up a note saying trainees must not use the lifts.
A guard checking every door would work.
But the simplest guarantee is a key that only opens the parts cupboard.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
A continuous integration pipeline gives its review agent one tool, manage_deployment.
It has an action parameter of plan, apply or rollback.
The review stage must run plan on every pull request.
But it must never be able to change production.
And the security team insists the guarantee cannot rest on the model following instructions.
What's the best design?
Take a second.
The answer.
Split it into a read-only deployment_plan tool, plus separate apply and rollback tools.
And grant the review agent only deployment_plan.
The technical name for the principle is the enforcement ladder.
Three rungs.
Rung one.
Withhold the capability.
The agent simply does not have the tool.
Rung two.
Deny it deterministically, in code.
For example, with a PreToolUse hook.
That's a small script that runs before every tool call, and can refuse it.
Rung three.
Validate a record after the fact.
And a strongly worded instruction?
It's on none of the rungs.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a description sentence saying "never call apply from review."
Why?
It loses immediately, because the stem rules out relying on the model.
Wrong: a PreToolUse hook that blocks apply and rollback.
Why?
It's deterministic, and far better than a prompt.
But it's second on the ladder.
It filters the risk at call time, rather than removing it.
Wrong: have the server declare readOnlyHint true.
Why?
That's doubly wrong.
Annotations like that are untrusted hints, never authorization.
And labelling a tool that can apply to production as read-only is simply false.
We'll come back to annotations in part four.
And hooks get their full treatment in the Claude Code configuration chapter.
There's an honest counter-argument here.
And the self-check asks for it.
What's the strongest case for keeping manage_deployment whole?
Cohesion.
Three verbs on one resource, with one identity model.
So one honest description covers all three.
The resolution is to split on the destructive path, not on verb count.
Plan stands alone, as the safe tool.
Apply and rollback go where they can be permissioned, annotated and audited apart.
Hold on to this line.
Split tools where the risk changes, then withhold the risky one.
A few schema habits round out this task statement.
They turn up inside answer options.
There are five.
One.
Give every parameter its own description, saying what is and is not accepted.
For example, that a search field does not accept Jira Query Language.
Two.
Enumerate closed value sets with enum.
That way, an invalid project key fails schema validation, instead of reaching your business logic.
Three.
Bound numbers with minimum, maximum and default.
And say when to raise the value.
Four.
Set additionalProperties to false, so unexpected fields fail validation.
And five.
Mark only genuinely required fields as required.
A search tool needs only its query.
But a tool whose whole job is to produce a record requires every field of that record.
Quick recap.
When do you fix a description, when do you add a prompt rule, and when do you add architecture?
Fix the description when the model is choosing the wrong tool, or calling the right one repeatedly.
Because that's where the choice happens.
Examples come second.
Prompt rules that name tools are almost always the distractor.
And architecture, meaning subagents or classifiers, is for when the job genuinely divides by role.
Not when two labels overlap.
That's part one.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
The description is the interface.
So say what the tool does, say what it does not return, and name the tool that does.
Coming up in part two: structured error responses for M C P tools.
